utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, to round off your testimony before the Court, yesterday when I saw the subjects raised by the Prosecutor, I thought I would have quite a number of questions. However, now that I went through that, I think it won't take much time, not more than ten minutes or so. Yesterday, the Prosecutor asked you about criteria laid down by Bozo Rajic concerning the work of the IPD service. The Croatian word "promotion" does not really mean "propaganda", does it? Do you know the difference between these two words?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The word "promotion" practically means promoting traditional Croat values. The other term, and that is what the Prosecutor had in mind, concerns propaganda. That is not that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is what I thought you would tell us, you promote virtues, and that is the gist of the meaning of the word "promotion", unlike the word "propaganda". Yesterday, you were asked also why and whose decision was it that prohibited the military in the HVO to engage in politics. I suppose that at any given moment during your military service, you had an opportunity of reading the decree on the armed forces of the HVO. Article 85 [sic] of the decree says that all political activity in the military force within the HVO is prohibited. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. However, when I spoke yesterday, I meant -- and I think that was the thrust of the Prosecutor's question, that there was a document which regulated this matter specifically, and I said that there was no such document. But what you are saying is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Merely for the transcript, what I meant was Article 25 of the decree, and the transcript says "85". I suppose it was a slip. Now we can move on. Mr. Prskalo, a great deal was said -- Your Honours, this decree on the armed forces, it was already adduced as Document D182/1. I was saying yesterday a great deal was said and the Prosecutor asked you a great deal about the relationship between the late Mate Boban and Mr. Kordic, and I suppose we should perhaps clarify this topic from a different angle. Mr. Prskalo, you were a member of the military wing of the HVO, that is, the Croat Defence Council, the armed forces; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can also agree, I suppose, that there was also a civilian wing of the HVO, that is, at the level of the Croat Community, that is, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO government headed by Jadranko Prlic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the same time at the municipal level, there were municipal HVO governments, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, and that is the area of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, at the same time there was one vice-president of the HVO government, that is, vice-president to Mr. Jadranko Prlic, Mr. Anto Valenta, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other hand, in the military organisation there was the main staff of the Croat Defence Council; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then operative zones, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already told us -- we don't have to repeat that -- that Mr. Boban was the president and at the same time the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were shown a document, Z223, referring to a session -- to a meeting of the leaders of the HVO, Central Bosnia, held on the 29th of February, 1992. You couldn't find your way around this document, but when I -- as I read it, I know I saw that Bugojno was represented at the meeting by the deputy president of the HVO, Anto Krajinovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He was present at the meeting, and I know that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A lot was said about this document and decisions of this document in relation to Travnik. It was put to you that the move of some of the offices of the Croat authorities to Travnik would have a bad effect on Muslims. Would you agree with me that the ratio between the Croat and Muslim population, that was about 50/50?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Not in Travnik only, but also in a number of other municipalities in Central Bosnia, the population ratio, statistically speaking, between the Muslims and the Croats was similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware, Mr. Prskalo, that in Travnik the police administration for Travnik had its seat there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police was there, and after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took Travnik, that seat moved to Vitez and also some other offices. To all intents and purposes, the crowd police was driven away from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Anto Valenta, whom we mentioned a moment ago, who was the HVO vice-president, also had his office in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, he used to commute to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, which is the capital of the Central Bosnian Zupanija?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at where the first man of the government was in that area, it is quite clear that it was Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both according to Vance-Owen Plan, and after Dayton, Travnik was envisaged, planned, to be become the capital of that whole region, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday also there was mention of the language, why would it be bad for Croats if the name of the language was changed. And I didn't really want to go into that, because it is very clear what it means to a people if the name of its language is changed. But would you know that the Bosnian Language Department at the Faculty of Philosophy in Sarajevo was founded only after the war, that is, only after 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, during re-examination, the rule is that counsel cannot lead the witness. It is the same as examination-in-chief. It's your own witness and you're not allowed to lead him. Now, I haven't stopped you before, but I must point that rule out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall abide by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. Do you know when the Bosnian Language Department was set up at the Faculty of Philosophy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the information that that department was founded, yes, practically after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian language exist before?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian language in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist before, and I can affirm with certainty that such a name did not exist ever; namely, in our history, at the time of Kalay during Austria Hungary yes, Kalay did make some effort to introduce the Bosnian language, but it was never translated into life. And I must tell you that such a language doesn't exist. These are merely attempts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not assisted by this sort of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Prskalo. Document Z233, and that is the one that was somewhat questionable yesterday, because; that is, the excerpt of the meeting of HVO leaders held on the 6th of October, 1993. I looked at the list of present, more or less -- not more or less. They were all either presidents or secretaries. Except you, more or less, all the rest of them were presidents of the HVO from Jajce, Fojnica, and then across the region. It was put to you yesterday -- I do not know whether the Prosecutor did not understand it, but it was alleged that you had been promoted by the fact that you became a member of the chair. But the chair, it is a one-time duty. What does the chair, that is, the working presidency, mean? What does it mean to be in the chair of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so how our language puts it, the chair, that is, the working presidency, or the chair, is a body which moderates a meeting. However, if I remember well, I responded yesterday and said that I was no member of the chair, because that body had not been elected by anyone to moderate the meeting. It was merely a conversation, a discussion, about some problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Another question. If somebody is a member of the chair, if somebody is in the chair of a meeting, when does his duty stop?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty of the chair ends the moment the meeting ends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is a civilian document in full, and it is signed. If you have the document before you, please look at the last page in the Croatian language. Will you look who are the signatories of the document. Can you find the last page in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the last page. It says that it is the vice-president of the government of HZ HB, Anto Valenta, and on the left-hand side the secretary. I can't really see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the name, if you can recognise the name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name below is Ignac Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday a great deal was said. I don't really want to go into it, but military matters were raised as a subject, in a broad sense of the word, in relation to a quotation from some speech, or rather of Mr. Kordic's. In your view, do military matters have a narrow meaning, or can they be placed in a broader context?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military matters may be viewed in a broader context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are other questions apart from this stricter issue of orders for a particular military combat which could then be placed in a wider context of military matters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from professional things when orders are issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question either, and it sounds to me like argument, which you can address to us in due course. Now, unless there's some specific matter for the witness, I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- no, all right. We can change the topic. I thought that perhaps we might hear it from Mr. Prskalo, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday a tape was shown and we could see some business outlets demolished, something to that effect. And you said that there were incidents on both sides, and you were an eyewitness to those incidents, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were incidents, on both sides. And often this was done by members of one people to members of others. Or sometimes a people did it to members of its own -- members of the same people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For various reasons, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday that motives behind that varied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, to your knowledge, insofar as the damage inflicted on business outlets owned by Muslims or Serbs, was it organised on the Croat side or were there acts committed by individuals?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information that there were any organised actions of that nature in our lands, and in my view, these were acts committed by individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Prskalo, you were asked who was your provisional commander, if I may put it that way, while Colonel Blaskic was in Kiseljak, and you said the head of the staff of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. You didn't give us the name, so let us try to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the staff of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was Mr. Franjo Nakic, who also was with me, part of the monitoring mission in Busovaca. I believe we noted that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on. Yesterday you were given a transcript of an alleged conversation between Dario Kordic, Mr. Dario Kordic, and Colonel Blaskic. And in contrast to what the Prosecutor is claiming, we believe that it is in dispute whether the two of them talked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in Kacuni right after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It's not in dispute that the voices on the tape were those of Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic. That has never been disputed. Are you trying to say now it's in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do not think that we ever said that that conversation took place. That was the thrust of my question. We are referring to the conversation. We are not questioning the voice of Mr. Kordic. As for Mr. Blaskic, I'm not quite sure because, I don't know his voice. It is the conversation that is at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is as follows, Mr. Prskalo: So you were in Kacuni after the ceasefire was concluded following January conflicts. Had these multiple rocket launchers attacked Kacuni, as it was suggested to you yesterday, would you see the results of that in Kacuni? Wouldn't you see that devastation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I was in Kacuni several times. If we're talking about this, I think that we also need to say something about Kacuni, that is, the part of the village which -- of the Muslim population, and I couldn't really see all those projectiles falling on it. I simply don't understand, had it really happened that way, I don't understand how could I miss that. I mean, there were also members of the monitoring mission. They went there. We went together. And then Muslims representatives and members of the monitoring mission of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not see any destruction?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any destruction of such a scale that would indicate such heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us move on to a different document, Z419.3, and that is a letter in your handwriting to the command of the brigade, do you remember, 30th of January, 1993? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. I saw that document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One can see from this text that it is self-evident that you are requesting that somebody be nominated to this Joint Commission, but my question is who is this addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is addressed to the command in Kiseljak, because we were asked to urgently designate a member to work in the Joint Commission, because we decided that there was no men available from that area and it was a general conclusion, the conclusion of everybody, that it would be good and that it would be purposeful if Kiseljak were included too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the letter was addressed to military structures, wasn't it, not to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, a short video was shown, Z652, and it was shot around the 13th of April or something like that, it is said. We're not quite sure. But the Croat National Council is mentioned in it. I suppose you remember who are the members of this council. The Prosecutor mentioned Dr. Komisic, Kljujic, and so on and so forth. Do you recall the efforts, the attempts, to set up this Croat National Council in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember some attempts to set up this National Council, but I couldn't really tell you exactly who were its members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then ask you this way: Could you tell the Court which political party of the Croats was the counterpart or, rather, the signatory or, rather, led the negotiations with the International Community and that eventually led to the Dayton Agreement, which party of the Croats was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to my knowledge, in the creation of that agreement participated the Croat Peasants' Party. I don't mean the Croat National Council that Kimisic was a member of, I mean the Washington and Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed it; do you know? The representatives of which party signed that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, the HDZ. If you mean which is the main party, then that is it. I didn't really understand what you were getting at, but it was the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kljujic was mentioned, his replacement, and so on and so forth. Did you have any direct knowledge, what was the meeting that removed him from office? Was it as before or did the practice change, that is, when Kljujic succeeded Perinovic, an earlier president of the party? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, he simply -- the majority simply -- there was not a vote of confidence in his favour. As far as I know, the majority simply did not place their confidence in him, and that was a democratic choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Z652A is another document. That is, if you remember, a fragment from a rather long letter which Mr. Kordic read between Mate Boban and Jadranko Prlic, that is, the views of the government of the HDZ on the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some parts of that fragment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, Mr. Kordic voiced some thoughts which I believe are self-evident, but I presume that you also took note of some of those observations and thoughts. It arises from the transcript that nothing will happen by force?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but from what I remember, no expressions nor terms were used to indicate any violence, any squaring of accounts. Quite the reverse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an obvious intention of resolving problems by political methods in order to avoid a conflict, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is another document. I don't know if you had enough time to go through that. Mr. Kordic was finishing, and the journalist said, "Thank you, Mr. Vice-President." Do you remember that detail from the record?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. If you mean the video, it wasn't shown to the end, and I didn't really read the record to the end. I only scanned a few sentences, because I really had very little time at my disposal to read all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let us go to this next document, Z671.1. The Prosecutor told you that in spite of this document, that you did not complain because of the attack to the other side, I mean, to Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, one of the explicit requests in the document is the request to terminate military operations. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what I wanted to say. That is what bothered me as of yesterday, because the Prosecutor did not yesterday permit me to answer that question. I'm really very happy that you are asking me that today, that you really took note of that. Namely, in these conversations, I said, without mixing words, that it was the army of B and H which had launched the attack against us, and I can't understand how -- responsible people who were sitting there with me must have taken note of that. I really don't understand how can it be that they did not note it down or did not report it higher up. It is simply beyond me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to round this off, Mr. Prskalo, you had the opportunity to see hundreds of orders issued by Mr. Blaskic or, I suppose, quite a number of other officers within their fields of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw quite a number of orders, but I couldn't, of course, see all the orders because I mostly had to deal with those orders which concerned myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But of all the orders that you saw, did you ever see any military order issued by Mr. Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I did not see such an order ever, I have never even heard that such an order had been issued or, rather, I simply do not know that Mr. Kordic ever issued any such order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, as I told you yesterday, you're of course in the best position to tell us. Did you ever, as Colonel Blaskic's deputy commander of the Operative Zone or, rather, assistant for IPD, did you ever issue any military orders or take part in the formulation of these orders in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to correct what you have just said. In my work, I was only authorised to write information. I simply had no authority to issue any orders. And I should correct what you said. I was not Colonel Blaskic's deputy. I was his assistant for IPD, and that is not one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree. My mistake. Assistant for IPD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said you would be ten minutes, Mr. Naumovski. You've been half an hour. Now, is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have just stopped me in time. I have finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Prskalo, for coming. Your evidence is now over. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. Was there a matter you wanted to raise while the next witness is being brought?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that the Court actually wanted to raise with us the status of the application that we've made for the Court to issue a request for assistance to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just update the Court on that. We would like to withdraw that request. We have encountered no difficulty at all in gaining the assistance of the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have a judge appointed for the purpose of authenticating affidavits, and in that regard we submitted our first affidavit yesterday of Brigadier Zviko Totic. That affidavit will be submitted, Your Honours, in corroboration of the testimony of one of the witnesses to testify next week, Brigadier Luka Sikerija. We had hoped that we would be able to call Brigadier Sikerija this week, and that's why we filed the affidavit yesterday. But apparently that's not to be. That leads me to one subject that I would like -- there are two issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal, first of all, with the affidavit question. It may be sensible to collect your affidavits, as it were, and we'll consider them as a group at a convenient moment. The advantage of that is that the Prosecution will then be able to decide whether they want to make any objections or not. Obviously, it's got to be done at a convenient time and at a convenient time for you too. But rather than doing them one by one, there may be an argument for putting a group in together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If that is to be the case, Your Honour, might I suggest that we have the argument earlier rather than later, because as we understand 94 ter, it is done on an affidavit-by-affidavit or case-by-case basis or, to be more accurate, a live-witness-by-live-witness basis, and an objection must be filed within seven days after a live witness testifies as to the affidavit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, I suspect you're right. We better do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just articulate a concern that we have at this point, if I may. Our estimate of completing our case by the August recess was based upon the assumption that the Prosecution would be accorded pretty much the same treatment as the Defence received for 11 months of its cross-examination of the Prosecution's witnesses, which was that, as a general rule, the time of the direct examination would govern the time available for cross-examination. We're obviously aware, Mr. President and Your Honours, that there were some exceptions to that. I can remember right now the witness Colonel Stutt who testified, I believe, for about one and a half hours on direct, and I think we took about two and a quarter hours on cross-examination. But the Court will recall that there were a lot of documents to be introduced through that witness and it was a rather laborious exercise. But I must observe that generally here, in fact in almost every case, the cross-examination of Defence witness is taking at least twice as long as the direct examination. I think that's true for every single witness. Now, we actually, in our estimate, Mr. President, we built in some time to assume that there would be, with respect to the first witnesses, a fairly extensive cross-examination, and I think notwithstanding the amount of time that's been taken to date, we're still pretty much on target for our estimate. But I might point out that a lot of the cross-examination just consists of argument with the witness, and I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, that is not so. If it were argument with the witness, it would be stopped. But I think you can take it that the Trial Chamber is with you on the various points you're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then I'll move on to the last point, Your Honour. It concerns the witness for whom we had made an application for a videolink, Srecko Kristo. Let me just explain. I think it's fairly clear to the Trial Chamber that we are trying to put on our witnesses in a thematic way. The last two witnesses that we have on the chain of command issues will be today's witness, Brigadier Totic, and the first witness after him, Brigadier Sekerija. After that, we propose to move on to the Kacuni checkpoint issues that have been raised by the Prosecution. Mr. Kristo, strictly speaking, does not relate to the January the 20th to 21st checkpoint incident. So he's not, strictly speaking, a part of that cadre, if you like, but he does offer evidence relating to an incident that occurred at the Kacuni checkpoint on the 24th. Now, I understood our application was denied, but let me just represent to the Trial Chamber that as of this point, we are not aware of any other witnesses that we intend to call who will give evidence by videolink. So it may be that at some point we would ask the Court again to consider such an application, hoping, I trust, that that doesn't fall afoul of the rule that generally motions for reconsideration will not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I should have made that plain, that the reason that it was denied was merely the timing and the need to make logistical arrangements. And, of course, the matter will be reconsidered. What we invited you to do was to group your witnesses. If you've only got one in Sarajevo, so be it. But if you've got others elsewhere, it may be convenient to try and deal with them all at the same time. What I suggest you do is to start making your list and then to approach the Registry, because it's a major logistical exercise to arrange this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The ramifications were explained to us yesterday, Your Honour. We had suspected that it was a major logistical exercise, but I have to confess that I did not realise quite how extensive it was. And we're mindful of the need for economies, both in terms of time and cost. But as I say, at this point, unless we can convince this gentleman to travel to The Hague, which may be very difficult, it may be that the only way that we can get his testimony before the Court would be by videolink. But he is, as I say, the only one of whom we are currently aware that we would anticipate testifying by videolink from Sarajevo. There may be one other witness who needs to testify through that medium in Zagreb, but we hope not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can investigate the matter and then identify a suitable time with the Registry and make your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just take one minute. By the order of the Trial Chamber of April 28th, I'm ordered to justify to the Trial Chamber the extensive number of the witnesses to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was hoping that I will be able to do that verbally and not be forced to write down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or is it too late now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will identify a convenient moment to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. I just want to be sure that you will call me, that it not is I who will not respect the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Nice, can we return to this question of cross-examination. You said in your submissions last week, or earlier this week, rather, that cross-examination was designed to assist the Trial Chamber, and of course it is. I think we have to balance the need for thoroughness, of course covering relevant matters, with a need for expedition in this case, and also, to some extent, the equality between the parties. I make no comment on the quality of cross-examination between the parties. As to why, speaking for myself, I may have been led to stop cross-examination during the Prosecution case because of doubts about its relevance. But that aside, clearly we should try and aim to run both sides in the same way. That is one factor which I would ask you to have in mind. The other factor is to invite you to reconsider the position about exhibits. To date, the total number of Prosecution exhibits, I understand, is 2.392. That, by any standards, is an extensive number. In fact, we could well consider that we're swimming in these documents. It's not of assistance, really, to have too many. So I'm not going to invite you to address us on the topic at the moment, but I would at this stage invite you to reconsider the question of exhibits, whether it's necessary to put more exhibits in, the Prosecution case having closed, unless they are particularly relevant, going to credibility or going to the witness's evidence, and also to consider tailoring the cross-examination. I say I'm inviting you to do it, which is all I am doing at the moment, but I have to say that in due course we will have to consider making orders. I hope that won't be necessary. The position is this: As I said the other day, we have three other cases, all of them lengthy, involving in some cases persons in custody, and we have not only this case but those other cases to consider. You, if I may put it this way, have had a year in which to bring the Prosecution case, and we have to consider cross-examination in that light and ask you to deal with the matter expeditiously. We do intend to complete Mr. Kordic's case by the recess, and in that we shall require your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour will have it. And I have to say, without in any way resigning from the points I've made earlier, it's my intention, and I'm sure that of all my colleagues, to be as brief as we properly can. The Chamber will have in mind -- and I'm not going to argue the point extensively at all -- but the Chamber will have in mind that the witnesses so far are the witnesses who cover the whole of the case. I think Filipovic, for example, basically covered the whole of the Blaskic and Kordic case, and I cross-examined him in a day. So these early witnesses are likely to be longer. I'm anxious myself to avoid adducing exhibits, and we'll be further cautious about producing exhibits, and I really don't forecast, I hope, too much need to do so. Can I turn from that to one other timesaving issue which I was going to raise myself in any event, and it relates to the evidence, particularly, for example, of the next witness, about Muslim atrocities and other bad acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the relevance of that is something that we've always doubted but we've never challenged, because it would seem to us to give the appearance of unfairness, perhaps, if we challenge the matter too vigorously, or at all. We leave it to the Chamber to confine evidence on those topics that is not thought to be helpful. However, where details are given, as they are, for example, in this summary, we will attempt to make an institutional or semi-institutional response at some stage to detailed allegations, and we've also had a list of stipulations on the same topic. The Chamber will realise I can't admit something in the sense that I'm not a party. I'm not here standing for any group of people; I'm only here for the OTP. So I can't admit something. I'm not the Muslims concerned. But I should be able, with a reasonable amount of time to discuss matters, I should be able to agree that certain matters can be taken as facts for the purposes of this trial only, and to that extent I hope that we can then abbreviate issues. What I can't do is simply turn it around over night, because there are considerations of an institutional nature that have to be taken in mind. But I'm certainly intending to do that, and I'm setting in train the procedures that will have to be followed if and when detailed allegations of the type that are raised in this sort of proof are capable of agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That will be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, on another matter, just -- totally different matter, the position on the audiotape, as the Chamber I think recollects, is that the voices were quite specifically admitted in a carefully thought-out process of offering the document for listening to and agreeing to the voices. And indeed, the Chamber will find somewhere, I think in an exchange with Mr. Stein, that it was made clear by me that the admission was not just a general admission but was an admission as to the two voices and the way they are associated with voices 6 and 7 on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I understand the Defence case, it is this: that the voices are admitted, but that in some way the authenticity of the tape is challenged, and that it's said that this conversation didn't take place in the way that it's alleged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I said initially there may be some difficulties. There was then a suggestion to odd words being added, and that's I think as far as we've got in detail. But I've always approached the two witnesses to whom I've put the tape on the basis that there may be some challenge to its authenticity, but the voices are accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I think that the position relating to the videotape is as stated by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The audiotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'm sorry. Yes, the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Secondly, with respect to the matter addressed by the Prosecutor, the Muslim atrocities, this is the last witness through whom we would offer evidence of the atrocities at Dusina. And I do recall an earlier exchange on this between the Court and Defence counsel where it was suggested that we prepare a short stipulation with no frills, just the bare bones, and we did that. And I have actually transmitted that. It consists of six paragraphs on about half a page. I transmitted that to the Office of the Prosecution, and I believe that's still being considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if you send a draft to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have one now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Send one to the Trial Chamber. Send it in due course to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- so we'll know what's being considered. Yes. On that topic, I had noted that out of the six witnesses, three already have mentioned Dusina, and I was going to invite you to think that that was sufficient on that. And also the other matter, which was the deaths of the children at Vitez. You've called three witnesses on that. Now, there comes to be a limit on these matters, as we've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, and we're mindful of that. There's only one other piece of evidence with respect to the children, and that's an actual videotape of the aftermath of that event, and we would propose to introduce that at this time. But as far as I know right now, we do not have any -- we actually have one other witness on that, the mother of one of the children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that not a sort of witness who could make an affidavit, rather than bringing her here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It may be, and I would not want to put her through that, especially if it required showing the videotape, which is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Other than that, though, Your Honour, I think the relevance of the evidence is as we've previously stated. It's really not the sort of tit for tat argument, the Tu Quoque argument. It's really evidence as to who was persecuting whom, what was going on in the area, and it's really relevant to the allegations made in count 1. And in respect of one of the judge's questions yesterday, I just mentioned paragraph 36, but with respect to the theory of a campaign or a policy or some sort of official party line, so to speak, those allegations are made actually in the earlier paragraphs of the amended indictment too, and the evidence is relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I said, I think the point has been made, and we don't need to make the point really anymore, other than with this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we will sit till a quarter past 1.00 today. We'll only take a 20-minute break. So it may be convenient if you go on for -- until quarter past 11.00, something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would anticipate that the testimony of this witness would last perhaps an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: My name is Zivko Totic. I was born on 25 January 1958, in the village of Dolac, in the municipality of Zenica, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to take you very quickly through some of the points in the outline that you've signed in Croatian, and the English version of which you've signed and initialled every page, sir. Is it true that you are a Bosnian Croat, that you're married and have one son, who will graduate from electrical engineering school this year?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You currently work at the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo as an advisor for the development of defence policy; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right that you have held the rank of Brigadier in the Army of the Federation since December 31st, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You currently own an apartment in Sarajevo, sir, but you're not able to live in it, either yourself or your family, because it is currently occupied by a Muslim refugee family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live during the week when you work, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: During the week I live in Hotel Dalmatia in Kiseljak, and otherwise I live in the town of Jajce with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you see them on weekends generally, or more regularly?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Mostly over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HDZ BiH?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of other questions in the hope of saving some time on cross-examination. Have you ever signed any statements to any institution or at the request of any attorney, other than the statements that you've signed in connection with this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that the first time that you and I actually met face to face was earlier this week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first time that you met my colleague, Mr. Naumovski, in person was this week, having had with him an earlier telephone conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have previously been interviewed by the investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor, have you not, a gentleman by the name of Stefan Obers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked to sign a witness statement by the investigator when he interviewed you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on to paragraph 6 of your outline, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with the Trial Chamber's permission, I propose to lead a large part of this evidence, except on controversial matters, and I'm sure I'll be told when we reach those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that you received your elementary schooling in the village of Stranjani, near the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after completing one year of vocational school for business in Zenica, you were accepted at the secondary military school in Sarajevo, which you successfully finished, or you graduated from that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you attended your last year of schooling at the military school, studying with the Engineering Corps training facility in the town of Karlovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, that you served for ten years in the Yugoslav People's Army as a noncommissioned officer initially?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first you commanded a squad, and then your duties increased in importance; you commanded a platoon in Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you were transferred to Sarajevo in July of 1988, and then in 1990 and 1991 you attended the higher military school for engineers in Karlovac and Sabac?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You completed your military training at the higher military school on December 4th of 1991, having also studied by that time statistics and computer science at the Department of Statistics in Belgrade; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I believe that on December 4th, 1991 you were promoted to the rank of second lieutenant and became the commander of a company of JNA engineers in Bihac, in the west of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the war broke out in your country, or when your country was attacked, when the civil war broke out, if I might be so bold, on April 26th of 1992 you resigned from the JNA and then moved back to your hometown in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I wonder, sir, if we could just have you testify in your own words as to what occurred after you had been -- after you had made the decision to resign from the JNA and returned to Zenica. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Shortly after my return to Zenica, and I believe it was on the 2nd of May, 1992, I was invited by the commander of the Crisis Staff of the Croat Democratic Union in the village of Stranjani, I was asked to attend a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the HDZ BiH in Stranjani, and we discussed their prompt and efficient establishment of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in Zenica at this time, were there any organised units of Croats, any organised military units of the Croat people in the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, in the territory of the Zenica municipality, there was something between five to ten platoons of the HVO organised. In contrast, in the town of Zenica and the municipality of Zenica, there were a number of Muslim formations. In early January 1992, the so-called 1st Brigade of the Territorial Defence was formed, headed by its commander Dzemal Najetovic. Shortly after that, a battalion of the Patriotic League, headed by Ibrahim Puric was also stationed in the town of Zenica. And the Patriotic League then came out into the public. I believe it began to come into existence sometime in mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Territorial Defence in Zenica was, in fact, a predominantly Muslim military organisation, consisting of about 97 per cent Muslim members; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: More than 97 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber your assessment, sir, your professional military assessment, of the quality of organisation of the Muslim military forces in Zenica at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The Muslim armed forces in Zenica in 1992 were -- well, I must say they were well organised, and personnel who had come from the former JNA mostly commanded their ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... referring to consisted of professional officers and noncommissioned officers previously serving in the former JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after you took over your military duties in Zenica, sir, could you explain to the Court what you did or what position you assumed in June of 1992, and what you did in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After I joined the Zenica HVO, I was first appointed the commander of the company in -- which was about to be formed, but it was never formed. After that, I was asked to form a battalion in the village of Stranjani, and I became its commander. I was successful in setting up this battalion sometime in the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I believe that on July 29th of 1992 Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, appointed you to be the commander of the HVO staff in the city of Zenica. Is that accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. But shortly afterwards I was issued the same order from the supreme commander of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were not appointed to your position by any civilian authority, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I was not appointed by any civilian authority to the post of the commander of the Municipal Staff. As it was said, I was first appointed by the commander of the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia, Colonel Blaskic, and after that by the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, who was at the same time the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And as the commander of the HVO staff in Zenica, you proceeded to reorganise HVO forces that were under your command in that city; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I began to reorganise them as soon as I took the office, sometime until mid-October. The municipal HVO staff was made up of three battalions, total strength about 1.450 men. My other task, apart from this and the training, was the formation of a combat group, some 60 to 200 men strong, which every 7 to 10 days took shifts at the front in Jajce. I need to mention that the HVO units at that time were fighting very fierce and bloody battles for the liberation of the town of Jajce. And in spite of the tremendous efforts invested by the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia to defend the town of Jajce, the Muslim units, in contrast, that is, the Territorial Defence in the first place, I think they did not send any significant, any noteworthy reinforcements to the town of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the subject of Jajce, just a few very brief questions. Is it correct that you were responsible for maintaining a sector of the front lines and that your specific responsibility in that connection was to rotate a group of soldiers back and forth to man the front lines against the BSA during that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: In November 1992, after the fall of Jajce, the army of Bosnian Serbs came dangerously near the town of Travnik, and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia decided to set up three sectors. I was appointed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you, the question was whether you were rotating groups of soldiers back and forth on the front lines before the fall of Jajce. Is that what you did? We can get into what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the fall of the town of Jajce on October the 30th, 1992, the position has been taken by the Prosecution in this case that two things happened; first, that the HVO basically abandoned the front lines and, second, that that abandonment was due to an agreement that was reached with the Bosnian Serb artillery to surrender the city. The town of Jajce, rather. Could you give the Trial Chamber, please, your personal experience with respect to either of those two arguments, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: About the agreements which existed or did not exist, I know nothing. But it is not true that the HVO units did not defend the town of Jajce. From the Municipal Staff of Zenica, troops, some 120 men commanded by Dobrica Jonjic, retreated on the 13th of October; that is, crossed the bridge over the Vrbas River. In contrast, the units of the 1st TO Brigade in the village of Kruscica and Busic, set up control points, and further on down to Turbe, while they were plundering and disarming other people or soldiers who were being pulled out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the town of Jajce fall as a result of voluntary withdrawal or military defeat, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Jajce fell because of the defeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the fall of Jajce on October the 30th, 1992, sir, could you just tell the Trial Chamber what your responsibilities became? And for the Trial Chamber's reference, it's paragraph 15 of the summary that you signed.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After the fall of the town of Jajce, I think it was November 1992 the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, decided, in order to put up a good defence of the town of Travnik, to form three defence sectors. I was appointed the commander of Sector 2. Its area of responsibility was from the Lasva River inclusive, across Turbe, Mosunj, Glavicica, Slikovica and Mravinjac to Kamenjas. My deputy was Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And it's correct, I believe, to say that on December the 4th of 1992, the HVO in Zenica was reorganised completely pursuant to a decision issued by the supreme commander of the HVO armed forces, Mr. Mate Boban; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of that reorganisation, could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what was implemented?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: As a result of this reorganisation, based on the order of the supreme commander, Mr. Mate Boban, I was appointed the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, and his decision of the 18th of December, '92, upon my proposal along the chain of command in the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, they appointed the command of the brigade of Jure Francetic by the commander of the staff of the HZ HB, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Jure Francetic Brigade was established as part of the early December, December the 4th, reorganisation decision issued by Mr. Mate Boban and that you were appointed as commander of that brigade pursuant to a separate decision that he issued later in the month on December the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Turning to subheading D of our outline, we have told you, sir, I believe, that the Prosecution in this case theorises that there was a widespread and systematic campaign of persecution directed against Bosnian Muslims in the municipality of Zenica first and also throughout each of the municipalities that comprised the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the existence or nonexistence of such a policy on behalf of Bosnian Croats in the area where you lived, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The persecution policy of Bosnian Muslims by Bosnian Croats, I learned about this policy only after I arrived in The Hague. The Croats did not persecute anyone. Quite the reverse. The Croats were the persecuted ones in Zenica and throughout the territory of the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to take you through this quickly, Brigadier. Did you ever, throughout your entire association with the HVO, ever receive an order from any superior officer or any kind of pressure, directly or indirectly, to harass or persecute any persons who belonged to any ethnic group other than Croats or to give those non-Croats any kind of a hard time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I never ever received that, nor did I ever hear about that. And had I ever received that, I can claim under full responsibility that I would not have complied with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true, sir, that Bosnian Croats in the municipality of Zenica were in a distinct minority?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: It is true that the Bosnian Croats in the town and the territory of the municipality of Zenica constituted a clear minority. In the territory and municipality of Zenica, Bosnian Muslims accounted for about 55 per cent, Bosnian Croats for about 15.5 per cent, and Bosnian Serbs accounted for about 15.4 per cent. The rest were Yugoslavs or members of other ethnic groups, and I believe they totalled something around 20.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just for the record, is it accurate that according to the 1991 census, as far as you can recall, the total population of the municipality of Zenica was in the region of 145.500, that about 80.300 or so were Bosnian Muslims, 22.500 or so Bosnian Croats, approximately 22.400 Bosnian Serbs, and about nineteen or twenty thousand Yugoslavs or others; is that accurate to say in a broad outline?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I just tried to cut it short and gave you percentages a while ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I appreciate that. After the civil war broke out, could you tell the Court approximately how many Bosnian Muslim refugees came into the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After the civil war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and after the fall of Eastern Bosnia, Bosnia and Krajina, a river of refugees streamed towards Central Bosnia and principally towards the town of Zenica. I believe that in '92 and until '93, something between thirty-five to fifty thousand refugees arrived in that area, mostly consisting of Bosnian Muslims. "Mostly", I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And we can all do the simple arithmetic. From a pre-war ratio of about four to one, the ratio of Bosnian Muslims to Bosnian Croats in Zenica had risen to about six to one by 1993; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, due to the influx. And I believe that it was planned, that it was a planned transfer of Muslim population to Zenica and the expulsion of Bosnian Serbs by Bosnian Muslims, so that their number went down to a mere 3.000. In the municipality of Zenica, the ratio between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats changed drastically. I think it was something about 120.000 to 20.000 Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 20 of your summary that to try to persecute people who were six times more numerous than the persecutors would have been stupid. Can you just elaborate on that point to the Trial Chamber, give them your views on that subject, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, to persecute an ethnic group which is six times larger than we were would be a theoretical and practical nonsense, and it simply could not be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You make some comments in paragraph 21 of your outline, Brigadier, regarding who it was that was -- well, you say that Bosnian Muslims were harassing and persecuting Bosnian Croats, and you give an example specifically relating to the first such expulsion of Bosnian Croats from their homes. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence about this already from Major Gelic, but could you just give, in a very encapsulated way, your recollection of that particular event, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Before the witness answers your question, I'd like to come back to the previous question about persecution. The witness said that it seemed to him that to persecute people that are six times more numerous than the persecutors would have been nonsense. I would like to ask Brigadier Totic whether throughout history you don't have examples of persecutions by minorities against majorities. Is it always the case that majorities persecute minorities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I know that there are such examples in history, but I also know what was going on in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I am absolutely clear about what was going on in the municipality of Zenica, and I affirm that Bosnian Croats never persecuted anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you indeed, Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just asking you some questions about the first example of a Bosnian Croat family being evicted from their home. I understand that you yourself sent your subordinate, Darko Gelic, to investigate that particular incident. Could you just explain, in a very short way, sir, the recollection that you have of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in August '92 a family came to me. They were a family of expelled Bosnian Croats from the place called Bistrica near Zenica, and they complained they had been evicted from their house by the Mujahedin. I believe they were called Kovacevic or Kovacic; I'm not sure. As soon as I heard that, I sent an officer from the staff command, Mr. Darko Gelic, to go out into the field and check the veracity of the complaint. After that, Mr. Gelic reported to me, saying that it was quite true that a family of Bosnian Croats had been evicted and that their house was right next to the training centre of the Territorial Defence. He also reported to me then that the majority of people in that centre were Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you observed and heard that TO troops regularly marched in full gear through Croat villages in the municipality of Zenica in a show of force?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It began as soon as the first TO brigade was formed up, that is, as of May '92, and those were -- that was one of their regular activities. All they wanted to achieve with that was to intimidate the Croat population in the territory of the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true that Croats were frequently evicted from their apartments in Zenica -- we've already heard from Major Gelic on that subject -- and that the Muslim-dominated wartime government discriminated against its Croat members in a number of ways?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber some examples of that, just to allow the Trial Chamber to have some concrete detail rather than broad generalisations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were a number of instances where Croats were evicted from their flats. They did not care for the office that somebody held. For instance, specifically in my command, in the brigade command, the family of Mr. Darko Gelic's, who was the officer responsible for intelligence affairs, the family was evicted from their flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it also accurate to say that as of April the 15th, 1993, both the TO and the HVO were legally-recognised military formations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is true that the HVO and the TO were equal military formations which made up the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to these two formations, there were also a number of paramilitary formations in the territory of Zenica municipality; in the first place, the battalion of the Patriotic League, which was the military wing of the SDA, then the Green Legion, headed by brothers Anabel and Ervin Barisic, and also HOS formations which at the time and later were comprised of more than 70 per cent of Bosnian Muslims. I perceived all these formations as paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, is the witness aware of any instances of evictions of Muslim families by Croats in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you've heard the Judge's question. Could you answer it, please?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, and I should like to hear one example. Could I be given one example, at least? And I'm quite convinced that there are none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm unable to provide one, sir. But let's continue on the outline here. Paragraph 24. You give an example of an attack against other non-Muslim ethnic groups, Serbs this time, by the Muslim armed forces, an attack in May of 1992 in the village of Drivusa. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber what you know about that particular attack, sir, and what you did after it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Sometime in early '92, that is, in early May, the Territorial Defence units from Zenica attacked an undefended village mostly populated with Bosnian Serbs. In that attack, in her house, which was at the entrance into the village of Drivusa, Ana Mitrovic, a Bosnian Croat, was killed. At that time, she was the mother of three minor children. Immediately after I became the commander of the Municipal Staff, and I believe that was on the 1st of August, '92, I publicly, over the media and in the media, condemned the attack on the undefended Serb village of Drivusa and the crime committed by the Territorial Defence units. I said, literally, that I would be ashamed if the HVO units had taken part in it. And the military and political leadership of Bosnian Muslims in the town of Zenica were quite indignant when they heard that statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Bosnian Serb population of that village of Drivusa, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb population from the village of Drivusa has been almost completely expelled, not only from Drivusa but from the territory of the municipality of Zenica. From 15.4 per cent, I think that the exact number of Serbs in Zenica were 22.433, only about 3.000 remained afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You're talking now about the entire city of Zenica, an exodus of about 19.000 Bosnian Serbs. But my question was actually related more narrowly to the village of Drivusa. What happened to the Bosnian Serb population of that particular village, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The village of Drivusa was expelled, as I've mentioned. However, some villages in the municipality of Zenica where Bosnian Serbs remained to live and who did not intend to move out, the representatives of those Serbs came to me to look for protection. Your Honours, at the cost of being called a Chetnik, I designated a platoon of 40 HVO soldiers to guard the village of Kozarci -- it was the hamlet of Lazic and the village Osojnica -- at night, and the population of those two villages was almost exclusively Serb. At the beginning, the HVO soldiers were very skeptical, but soon -- and the time showed this, that I was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just skip over, in the interests of time, paragraph 26, and go straight to paragraph 27. I'm not going to ask you specifically, Brigadier, about the murder of 12 Croats in Zenica, other than to ask you whether you prepared a contemporaneous document that recorded those events. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just show you a document that we have marked as one of the very few exhibits that we have for you, and I'd like to have this distributed, if I may, and request a Defence exhibit number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D209/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, very briefly, is this a document that you prepared? Or at least you'll see at the end of it there's the Croatian original, and that appears to be your signature. I would like you to confirm for the Trial Chamber that it is.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's no need to put that on the ELMO. The document says what it says, and we can all read it for ourselves. Following the events at Dusina, Brigadier, could you just tell the Trial Chamber whether there were any visits by bipartisan delegations, if you like, to that village, and if so, were you there, what did you hear, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as the crime of Dusina -- in Dusina is concerned, I was in Donje Panje [phoen] near Travnik at the command post when I heard about it. I immediately set out for Zenica and contacted the TO headquarters in Zenica, Mr. Jasmin Saric. Also, the president of the Zenica HVO and HDZ, through his lines of communication, contacted Mr. Djidic and Mr. Besim Spahic, who was the Zenica municipal assembly president. The negotiations were very sluggish, but after a while it was decided that the Lasva and Dusina villages would be visited by the joint delegation of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs. I was appointed to it as commander of the HVO, Jasmin Saric as the TO commander, Josip Pojavnik as the HDZ president, and Mr. Fuad Djidic as the SDA president in Zenica -- I believe he's now a consul in Australia -- president of the HVO, Dominik Sakic, and the head of the Zenica municipality, Mr. Besim Spahic, who I believe now is an Bosnian ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Turkey. With his request and with my approval, a journalist joined us, Mr. Andrija Tunjic, who worked for the newspaper Vjesnik from Zagreb. When we arrived in Lasva and upon entering the room where the meeting was being held, I saw a man carrying in some things. He opened the door, I approached him, and it was clear that the Croatian houses were being looted. I asked him what was going on, and he said that he had been ordered to collect things from Croatian houses and that these things would later be returned. I'm not aware that any of these things were later returned. In the meeting, I publicly asked Mr. Besim Spahic, the head of the municipality of Zenica, about this. He said nothing, and he just gave me a cynical smile which I will never forget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually, yourself, visit the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After this meeting and based on an agreement, the delegation was supposed to go to the village of Dusina. But the Muslim part of the delegation, led by Besim Spahic, refused to go to the village of Dusina, citing as an excuse that their car was not able to negotiate the steep incline. So Mr. Andrija Tunjic, Mr. Sakic -- there was a driver and his name was Tunjic [sic] -- and I went up there. When we came to the area of the hamlet of Dusina, which was a Croat hamlet, we were stopped by a member of the TO. I believe it was a local soldier from the village of Lasva. He immediately warned Andrija Tunjic that he was not allowed to take any pictures. He knew that we had been announced. I started a conversation with him, and I asked him what had happened. He made excuses that it was not them who did this, meaning the local Muslim population, but that this was done by elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade, 17th Krajina Brigade, and the 305th Brigade. After we entered the village of Dusina, I saw that there were seven Croat houses with 35 members and one Serbian house with eight people living there, and everything was burned. And Tunjic published this, his account of this, in a book a year later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think we need any more detail, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber will be grateful to know that that's the last evidence we have on Dusina, with the exception of properly authenticated death certificates, which we'll offer in due course and we need not take up time on that today. Let me just address, you to two other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on to a new topic, that might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Three very short matters. First, we have presented the death certificates, and at this point I'd like a request to have a Defence Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Exhibit is going to be numbered D210/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the second and third are transcript errors. Unfortunately, our LiveNote is not working, so I can't ascertain what the precise page and line numbers are, but perhaps we can clear it up this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you earlier testified that the bipartisan delegation that visited the village of Lasva consisted of Bosnian Croats, and you said -- at least the transcript says "Bosnian Serbs". Did you mean Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: That was evidently a mistake in the transcript. It was a joint delegation of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims, and I also gave the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And a final clarification. You referred to the 305th Brigade as one of the three military formations identified by the Muslim soldier that you met in Dusina. Is that the proper name for that brigade? Is it known as the 305th Jajce Brigade or Jajacka Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The number is 305, and it was also known as the Jajce Brigade, with its command near the village of Lasva. Immediately after the fall of Jajce, its headquarters were at a place called Biljesevo.
