utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had arrived at paragraph 28 of your summary, Brigadier. I wonder if you could just tell us what happened at the Cajdras checkpoint on March 28th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, 1993, at the Cajdras checkpoint, two military policemen of the HVO were killed. Their names were Bernard Kovacevic and Ivo Laus. On the same occasion, a Mujahedin was also killed. The incident, or rather the gunfire, started when a motor vehicle, a truck, with plates of the defence centre, refused to stop, and when those who were in the vehicle opened fire on the military policemen. Immediately after that, I sent the brigade officer, Darko Gelic, to the scene of the incident, and he told me that Mr. Jasmin Saric was there also representing TO headquarters in Zenica. And at a higher level, the scene of this event, two or three hours later, was also visited by Mr. Dobrica Jonjic. I believe at the time he was deputy commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police. And Mr. Dzemal Merdan, who at that time was the commander of the regional headquarters of Zenica TO. After that, Mr. Dobrica Jonjic, in a conversation with me, said that General Merdan had told him that an incident had taken place, had happened, because the HVO soldiers were refusing to allow the TO to take their weapons and equipment through the checkpoints and that they could not allegedly defend themselves because we were preventing them from getting weapons. Dobrica Jonjic then asked, "Well, is this also an HVO soldier showing the Mujahedin?" And Dzemal Merdan immediately retreated and said, but he is not one of ours."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And we'll hear more about Colonel Merdan later on. But let me just move on in the outline to the next day, March 29th, 1993. I believe there was an incident on that day, and I wonder if you can tell the Trial Chamber about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of March, 1993, an HVO soldier was killed from the 1st Infantry Battalion from Cajdras. His name was Slavko Pudja. He was killed in a facility where a squad of soldiers were spending the night. According to the investigation which was conducted the next day -- that is, that night and the next day -- as there was snow outside, one could see that the footsteps led to the villages of Preocica and Lupac, which are in the territory of the municipality of Vitez. The village of Vjetrenica is on the brow of the hill, on the boundary between the municipalities of Zenica and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any request made for an investigation into the circumstances of this killing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I asked the commander of the TO staff to investigate the circumstances of the murder, but nothing was done whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move to the next item on the outline. There's been a contention made by the Prosecution in this case that certain transit charges, or per-head transit charges, were charged by the HVO or by Bosnian Croats to permit expelled Bosnian Serbs from the Zenica municipality to transit through Croat-held territory to I believe the Ilijas municipality, just north-west of Sarajevo. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of it. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met a gentleman by the name of Dragutin Cicak?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dragutin Zvonimir Cicak was a man I met in the autumn of 1992. On that occasion a delegation of the 314th Brigade of the Army of BH, which was -- which came from the 3rd Corps had announced that they would come to see me in my command, and he arrived then with the commander of the 314th Brigade. I believe his name was Mr. Smajlbegovic, Suad Smajlbegovic. He introduced himself to me. He said he was a member of the command, and I believe he was in the department in the section responsible for the morale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clear up the record a little, Brigadier, when you say, "He introduced himself to me," are you referring to Mr. Smajlbegovic or to Mr. Cicak?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Cicak, because that was the first time that I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was Mr. Cicak in civilian clothes or in uniform, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, I remember well, was wearing a uniform with the insignia of the Army of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just relate the conversation that you had with this gentleman to Their Honours, please, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, this was a short conversation. At first glance, I thought it was a rather unstable person, because without no cause whatsoever, he immediately began to talk to me about Mr. Dario Kordic. However, nothing was founded in all his story. He voiced a number of accusations and pejorative remarks about Mr. Dario Kordic. Until that day, I did not know Mr. Cicak, nor did I know why was he attacking and expressing himself so deprecatingly about Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move fairly quickly through paragraph 32, Brigadier. You've already said that you dispute the story that a transit charge per head was imposed upon Bosnian Serbs who were trying to pass through Bosnian-Croat-held territory. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber why that is the case, why you dispute this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I dispute this because I claim, under full responsibility, that at no time was there a plan to dislocate or, rather, remove the Serb population from the Zenica municipality. Quite the contrary; I believed, and I believe this still, that the only way was to keep the Serb population in the territory of the Zenica municipality. After the Serb population moved from the territory of the Zenica municipality, the forms of pressure against the Croat population to move out became ever more intensive. I claim under full responsibility that the Zenica HVO and, as far as I know, the HVO of Central Bosnia, never had any plans, nor did they do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll -- a witness in this case, Mr. Cicak, has claimed that the articifer of this plan to impose transit charges was Mr. Dario Kordic. We'll speak about him a little bit later in your testimony, sir, but is such a plan consistent with Mr. Kordic's personality, or what you knew of Mr. Kordic from your knowledge of him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Dario Kordic, he could not have conceived of such a plan, as a man, or even think of it. Quite the contrary; Mr. Dario Kordic -- and everybody in Central Bosnia knows that -- advocated coexistence of all the inhabitants of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me move forward in time a little bit to April of 1993. You were, in fact, the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica in April of 1993, immediately before your abduction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether the HVO had any plan for offensive action against the ABiH or Muslim armed forces at any time in April of 1993, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Insofar as I'm aware, Your Honours, at that moment the HVO had no plan of any kind, nor was it planning any combat operations against the army of Bosnian Muslims. At that time, on the 14th, or rather 15th of April, 1993, the HVO, not only the one in Zenica but also for Central Bosnia, was not prepared for any combat operations; least of all was it prepared logistically. Let me remind you that at that time in the HVO of Zenica, as the commander of the brigade, I had armament for only about 30 per cent of the troops, that is, about 370 barrels. And of those weapons, no weapon was complete, no set, no combat kit was complete, so it would have been insane to think of something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, Brigadier, has already heard considerable evidence about the incidents that immediately preceded the outbreak of fighting on April 15th or 16th, 1993. You were aware, I take it, that a number of senior officers within the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade were kidnapped on April 13th, 1993 by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade outside of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that on the 13th of April, 1993, three officers of the HVO Stjepan Tomasevic Novi Travnik Brigade were abducted. I know all those three officers. Kambic, Sliskovic and Kovac are their last names. Subsequently --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need any further testimony on that, because we're going to hear from Mr. Kambic, who was one of those abducted officers, Brigadier. But let me just address a broader subject. Was there any kind of policy, as far as you could see, aimed at deliberately kidnapping senior officers in HVO armed units, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe, and I think, that there was a policy of abduction of HVO officers conceived by Muslim military representatives, and it came true at a later stage. It is my opinion that they consciously were trying to leave HVO brigades without their commanders so as to gain control over the territory more easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the three staff officers that you've identified, sir, is it also the case that a fourth HVO soldier, who was the driver of those staff officers at the time of their abduction, was himself kidnapped along with the three officers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to turn our attention to the incident in which you were kidnapped and in which your guards were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have a brief videotape, Your Honours. We've already provided it to the technical booth. I would anticipate that it would only last a minute and a half or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before we show that videotape, Brigadier, could you just describe to the Trial Chamber what happened to you on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, as I went to work, as usual, in the area of the village of Podbrijzje, the vehicle in which I was riding -- I believe it was Audi 100 -- a motor vehicle came straight at it. I believe it was about 5 or 10 minutes to 8.00 in the morning. And the driver said to me that a fool was coming at us. I raised my head -- I think I was just putting an audio cassette in -- and I saw the vehicle heading straight for us. And I said, "Well, let's try and go around it." The driver slowed down. I think we were driving at about 30, 40 kilometers per hour. There was a mild slope, and he wanted to go around the vehicle. But at that moment, from the vehicle, which was heading straight for us, very fierce fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court what happened to the person that was actually driving the car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I think that in that fire, one of the first bullets hit the driver directly in the head. His name was Ivica Vidovic, and he fell against my left side. That same moment, the escort -- his name was Tihomir Ljubic -- said to a soldier whose name was Anto, "Anto, look after the commander," and the soldier protected me with his body. He simply lied over me. And the other escort, Marko Ljubic, he told him to jump out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true that the person that was protecting you or shielding you with his own body was actually your brother-in-law, your wife's brother; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you were yourself hit by a gunshot to the head and that you still bear the scar of that wound today. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this attack on the vehicle, everybody was wounded. I believe that in that moment only Ivica Vidovic, the driver of the vehicle, was fatally wounded. All the rest were showing signs of life. I was also hit in the head, and as I was bleeding and I was dazed, soldiers who wore masks dragged me into the other vehicle. After I was placed in the other vehicle, I was -- my hands were tied behind my back with a type of handcuffs which are called Indians. You put -- if you put them in the water and if it gets wet, it will tighten in time and it will render your hands completely numb. Then they covered me with blankets -- with a blanket, and on each side of me a soldier sat down, and this is how they drove me in the direction of Zenica. Then there I was taken out of the car. I could only -- I saw a bridge there, and I was transferred to another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... that, but were you present when the people that were attacking your entourage and you fired bullets into the car from which you had been taken or snatched?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I was sitting in a vehicle. The driver was driving. All my soldiers were behind. After the killing of the driver, I said that the escort called Tihomir Ljubic, who was in charge of my security, and I quote him, "Anto, cover the commander. Anto, jump out." And I believe that by then the bursts of fire were coming from all sides. I don't know from which side they didn't shoot. I saw that one of the escorts called Marko was hit as he was stepping out of the car, and he was on the left-hand side. But at that moment, he was only wounded. After I was moved -- after I was taken to the other vehicle, I heard a terrible fire, and I believe that the three wounded soldiers were then killed in a most brutal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was this while they were in the car?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was this while they were in the car? While they were wounded, they were shot in the car; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. One soldier, I remember his name was Marko Ljubic, he had stepped out. He was sitting on the left-hand side, and he had just stepped out and he was hit as he was stepping out. He was just about to get out or he was getting out. The rest of us were all in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: With the benefit of hindsight, you would say that the purpose of this attack was to abduct you, rather than to kill all the persons who were in the car?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Now and even at the time of my abduction, it was clear to me that the goal was my abduction and the execution or the -- of all the witnesses. On this occasion, in addition to four HVO soldiers, a Bosnian Muslim was also killed, the father of six, who accidentally was there on his way to work in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might ask the technical booth to show the videotape, I'll just ask the Brigadier to confirm that this is an accurate depiction of the scene of events that he's just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that should be enough, I think, to get the picture. Thank you. That's enough, thank you. Could we get an exhibit number for the videotape, first of all, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 211/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm, Brigadier Totic, that that is a videotape of what occurred to you and your escorts on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber what happened after your guards had been executed, and the passerby shot dead, and after you had been kidnapped by the people that had attacked you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After I was abducted, they took me outside of the town of Zenica. We drove for about 30 to 40 minutes. I was held prisoner for 33 days in a family home throughout this time in a room where I was placed. There were guards. I believe that they were 3rd Corps soldiers. In the same room, there was a piece of furniture which was moved away from the wall, and I was handcuffed, and this is how I spent 33 days. They took off my handcuffs for the first time after 30 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you actually identify your abductors in any fashion, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot identify my abductors accurately. Throughout my stay in this family home where I had been taken and kept imprisoned, I saw the face of only one man, and it was an Arabic man; I could recognise that. But before and after that, no soldier who came to me ever showed their face. They were wearing masks, and also they wore gloves. I realised that it was not only Mujahedin but it was a wider plan conceived, I believe, at the top and at least in the 3rd Corps of ABiH. As proof of this, after my release I was told that at the intersection of the village of Podbrijezje there was a 20-millimetre gun mounted on the vehicle, and at that time, from what I know, the Mujahedin were not an independent and a separate unit of the ABiH and they did not have this weapon. This weapon was the weapon belonging to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Brigadier. This is, for the Court's information, paragraph 37 of the summary. Were any members of the International Community, members of the Red Cross or any other humanitarian organisation, permitted to see you at any point during your incarceration?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No, nobody visited me during my incarceration, no representatives of an international organisation or the International Red Cross. And I know, as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just restrict your answers to the question, please, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on a broader base, Brigadier Totic, were you aware that any members of the Red Cross or of the International Community were permitted to register or visit other detainees in facilities such as the music school in Zenica, detention facilities run, I believe, by the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they ever visited those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I will not dwell on this, Your Honour, because we actually have one of our witnesses, someone who was a detainee in the music school, and he can explain to you for himself what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of what happened to you, Brigadier, during your detention, could you just explain to the Trial Chamber the interrogations that you were subjected to and the circumstances under which those interrogations occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: In those 33 days of my imprisonment, I was interrogated two or three times. Before each of these interrogations, I would be ordered to kneel down. Around my neck they would wrap about a metre of fuse, which was taped to 200 grams of a powerful explosive, Trotil. And on the other side, they had an electrical detonator, and one of the army soldiers, my abductor, held the conductors and the battery which would have lit this fuse. As I was trained in explosives, I knew that these were real explosives and I knew they were activated, that I would be beheaded. But I also knew that they would not dare do it, because this was a room which measured three by four, and if they had activated it, they also would suffer serious consequences. During my interrogations, they were mostly interested in military and also political matters. They thought and they forced me to admit that Dario Kordic was the commander. I knew that he was not, so I couldn't say that, even if they killed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get into that in just a second, sir, but is it true that you were released finally from detention on May the 17th, 1993, as part of an overall agreement between the HVO and the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a general agreement on exchange, but I know that the HVO and the ABiH 3rd Corps agreed, with the assistance of Ambassador Thebault and also the German representative Salznik [phoen], and I believe that this is why we remained alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't believe there is any more need to go into that. For the Court's information, the circumstances of this prisoner release have already been identified in D79/1. The next subject which I would like to address with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, before you move on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you move on to the next subject, I would just like to clarify what you identified to the President this morning as the broad purpose of your adducing evidence of Muslim attacks on Croats. You said it was not in the form of a Tu Quoque direct response to the Prosecution case but rather, if I understood you correctly, by adducing this evidence of Muslim attacks you are seeking to cast doubt on the Prosecution's case of attacks by Croats on Muslims. You're seeking --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your aim is to make less credible the Prosecution story of attacks by Croats on Muslims; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The position is this, Your Honour, if I may, if I understand your question: Through this witness, obviously in the municipality of Zenica, I confess I do not particularly understand what the Prosecution's case is, because if the position that the Prosecution is advocating is that there was an attack by Bosnian Croats against Bosnian Muslims in that municipality, then frankly I think that that's misconceived and factually wrong, and I think that the evidence that has been produced in the last week has absolutely exploded that theory. But insofar as the broader case is concerned, the theory that's being advocated is that there was a systematic and widespread policy of persecution, or a campaign of persecution as I think it's referred to in the amended indictment, solely by Bosnian Croats waged against Bosnian Muslims, and we believe that that simply is not the case. We're not defending and we don't seek to defend the excesses committed by troops of the HVO during this very bitter and extended civil war, but we simply are trying to put before the Trial Chamber the full picture that there were evil actions going on both sides and that that was really, unfortunately, the times. It wasn't the result of a particular policy that was, if you like, imposed upon or squeezed into the hearts of Bosnian Croats by their leaders -- this was a civil war, unfortunately -- and not the result of any kind of top-down theory of the type that has been speculated by the expert witnesses that have testified before Your Honours; Dr. Donia being one example, Dr. Allcock being another. And at various times, I think, through the testimony of various witnesses, an explanation is sought to be -- well, I won't use the word "concocted", but an explanation is sought to be developed to try to impose some rationale upon an essentially irrational series of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand what you're saying. It's a fine point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, but thank you for asking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just go on, Brigadier. The next subject is Mr. or now Brigadier General Merdan, I believe. When did you first meet this soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I met General Merdan in mid-1992 in Zenica while he was the commander of the District Staff of the Zenica TO. After that and after the Washington Accords were signed, that is, two or three months after that, we were part of the HVO delegation. I was the president of the military executive committee of the HVO, and he was the -- he had the same post with the ABiH, and we worked in Uskoplje on the implementation of the Washington Accords. After that, I had an opportunity to get to know him better after '97, when we worked in the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina together until the April of this year, when he took retirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Brigadier. I don't want to take too much time on this subject, so let's try to move through it with speed so that we can fulfil our time estimate for the Court here. It's true that Colonel Merdan was never the official commander of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, but could you give the Court your understanding of what his functions within the 3rd Corps actually were, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Merdan was never the commander of the 3rd Corps. Commanders of the 3rd Corps changed. At first it was Hadzihasanovic, then it was Alagic, then it was Mahmuljin. But throughout this time, Dzemal Merdan was the deputy commander and acted as a shadow commander. I had a number of opportunities to satisfy myself that he was respected by commanders not only in Zenica but from Travnik to Uskoplje, and in my opinion he was the link between the political leadership of Bosnian Muslims and the 3rd Corps of the army. I also know that Dzemal Merdan was one of the founders of the Patriotic League, which is the military wing of the SDA, the Bosnian Muslim political party in Bosnia, and it is also clear to me that throughout the time of his stay in the 3rd Corps, he was an essential link between the 3rd Corps and the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the connection between then Colonel Merdan and the 7th Muslim Brigade, as far as you understood it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, and it is generally known, that Dzemal Merdan was one of the key organisers of the 7th Muslim Brigade. The 7th Muslim Brigade was founded and composed of soldiers from the then liberated territory, the territory that at the time had not been occupied by the Bosnian Serb forces. It was not a local unit, it was a unit established for quick and offensive tasks. And throughout the war, we had ample opportunities to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just turn your attention specifically to June of 1993, during the offensives that were launched by the ABiH in the Lasva Valley and in the Kakanj area. Is it the case that the 7th Muslim Brigade would be found deployed on the front lines of those offensives in villages such as Maljine, Cukle, Brajkovici, Susanj and Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the same true of the offensives later launched by the ABiH where the 7th Muslim Brigade was in the forefront of the attacks on Bugojno and Fojnica in July of 1993 and in Vares in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Not only those towns but Kresevo, where one of the commanders was seriously wounded. That was Serif Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have a conversation with General Merdan in connection with your detention by Mujahedin and a ransom note I believe he may have delivered to a witness who has already testified in this case, Colonel Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on several occasions I talked to Dzemal Merdan regarding my abduction. I was aware that he was not going to divulge anything significant in these conversations. But on one occasion while he was upset during negotiations in the BritBat in Uskoplje, he said, "Why didn't we kill you while you were in our hands?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to paragraph 45. I believe you had several conversations with Dzemal Merdan about Busovaca and its people while you were travelling from Sarajevo to Budapest in March of 1999. Could you just describe in very brief details those conversations to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I travelled both to Budapest and Vienna with Dzemal Merdan, to conferences and seminars, in a car, and on those occasions we had a chance to discuss and debate things very widely. In addition to his recollections of things from his youth, occasionally he would attack, in a rather insensitive way, anything that was Croatian in Busovaca. I concluded that this was a man who simply did not like Busovaca or its citizens, and that he was especially hostile to Dario Kordic. He was telling me how he had allegedly been detained for a day or two and beaten up by some HVO soldiers. He also told me that he knew everything and that he even knew which soldier hit him in the head. And all the blame he put squarely to Dario Kordic. And I said, "Well, why is Dario Kordic to be blamed, if you know exactly the names of the soldiers who beat you?" He remained silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever able to come up with any specific facts at all to support his allegations about Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: He never had any concrete facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the subject of Mr. Kordic, paragraph H of your outline on page 12. Could you just give your assessment of Mr. Kordic's position in Central Bosnia to the Trial Chamber, and please do it, sir, in a fairly abbreviated fashion, because the Court has already heard a lot of evidence from military witnesses along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: After the communist single-minded thinking and the introduction of a multiparty system, Bosnia and Herzegovina, like many other states, became the scene of the democratic processes, and it was at that time that Dario Kordic began to be politically active. For me, in particular, and for the Croat population in Zenica, Dario Kordic was a hope, because after so many years he had restored the self-confidence in the Croat population in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were aware that he held certain political posts within the HDZ BiH and within the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Dario Kordic held offices in the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he was one of the vice-presidents of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. I also know, Your Honours, that at no moment was Dario Kordic part of the military structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one of the problems with that, sir, is that occasionally Mr. Kordic was referred to as a colonel. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, from your own personal experience with the HVO, whether this Colonel Kordic, or Mr. Kordic, had any military powers or authority that you could ever see or that you ever witnessed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I claim, under full responsibility, that I do not know and that I have never seen Dario Kordic enjoy any military powers or command units. And as for ranks, how they were conferred upon various people, I can give you my example. On the 26th of April, 1993, I was indicated, I was named in an order as a colonel. However, I received the decree of my promotion to colonel only a year and two days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was while you were still being detained by the people that you've previously testified about; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you ever heard of a group called the Mixed Military Working Group that met at Sarajevo airport at the end of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I have heard that that Mixed Military Group was engaged in negotiations and that Mr. Dario Kordic was in it. According to the general idea, the negotiations at the time, and that was also requested by the International Community, the negotiations were to be conducted by military persons. But we did not have an army. In order to be able to negotiate, ranks were conferred upon people overnight. At the same time, no office in the army was held by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is that your explanation for the development of Mr. Kordic into an instant colonel, for purposes of being able to participate in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you've already testified about what the abductors who interrogated you tried to make you admit, and there's no point in going over that again. But I would like to ask you whether you ever saw or heard of Mr. Kordic having any authority, ability, or power to give military orders at any time.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No. Never, ever did I hear anything like that, nor was I ever issued any order by Dario Kordic. I did not get such an order, and as far as I know, nobody else did either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A question has previously been posed to a military witness that if Mr. Kordic had tried to give an order, what would the witness have done? What would you have done, Brigadier Totic, if Mr. Kordic had tried to give you a military order?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I would have returned that order to the structure of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. All the orders that I ever received, I received from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. There was the chain of command, and the principle of subordination there is also quite clear. And the policy about the issue of orders or instructions is also quite easy to discern, because there is the Ministry of Defence, and such policy always goes through the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a single written order of a military type issued by Mr. Kordic to any unit of the HVO, including the military police or any special purpose units, or did you ever hear of such a development?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Neither heard nor saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Brigadier, during your work, did you get any document concerning the strategy that was to be pursued in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never received such a document. And according to you, who was it that laid down the strategy that was to be pursued in the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, to my mind, as a soldier, the strategy is clear. The strategy is created and carried out from the top. The Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna at that time, and as of mid-1992, had the rules governing the conduct of the armed forces of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. We had our supreme commander, and at that time it was the president of the presidential council, Mr. Mate Boban. At that time we had a defence department, with the headquarters in Mostar, and it was headed by Mr. Bruno Stojic. The strategy, I believe, was designed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, to your mind, what were the relations between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Mate Boban? Where was Mr. Kordic's place in relation to Mr. Mate Boban, who, as you are telling us, was the supreme commander, and he was the one, therefore, who defined the strategy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I know is that Mr. Dario Kordic was one of the vice-presidents of the HZ HB, and I also know that throughout the time he was in Busovaca. And what was the relationship between the president, Mr. Mate Boban, and Mr. Dario Kordic, I simply do not know anything about it. Personally, I have never had an opportunity of even meeting Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you occasionally see Mr. Kordic giving speeches over the television, or hear him giving speeches over the radio, or see him giving speeches in person, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On rare occasions when I watched TV and listened to the radio, because I spent most of my time in the battlefield, I did listen to Mr. Kordic's speeches. I was also present on several occasions, mostly on the occasion of some anniversaries. When Dario Kordic delivered speeches, I did not see anything bad in his speeches. Quite the contrary; to my mind, these speeches were positive and I believed them to be in the service -- they were serving to create a front against the aggression of the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever give any speeches which made derogatory comments about members of other ethnic groups, as far as you can recall, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Insofar as I'm aware, he did not do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just turning to the last subject on your outline on the last page. Once again, Brigadier, the Court has already heard quite a bit of evidence regarding how the HVO was formed in April of 1992 and how the military arm of it and the civilian arm gradually grew into separate organisations with their own separate chains of command. Could you just give, in a thumbnail sketch, in two or three minutes, please, your views on that development to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The establishment of the HVO took place in April 1992. At the outset, the political and military functions in the HVO were rather closely interrelated. But as I said, the Peoples Gazette of the HZ HB, I believe, of July 1992 were given the rules of conduct of the armed forces, of the HZ HB, signed by the then-president of the HZ HB, Mr. Mate Boban, and the rules defined clearly and separated, distinguished, between military and political functions in the HVO. Those documents, and those adopted subsequently -- the discipline, or rather to improve the discipline in the HVO, district military courts were set up with district military Prosecutors. For Central Bosnia, the district military court had its seat in Travnik, and the district public Prosecutor was likewise, or rather the office of the district military Prosecutor, was also in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the last subject and the last exhibit. As a brigade commander, it's right, isn't it, that you were able to impose disciplinary punishments of up to 30 days of custody upon soldiers who had committed military infractions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of responsibility where I was the commander, I had this authority and I used it. The commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia had the authority to pronounce a higher disciplinary section, up to 60 days of imprisonment. I, as a brigade commander, I could pronounce the punishment, including 30 days of detention. Before that you have the reprimand, the warning, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two final questions, sir. Could you explain in your own words what role, if any, in the administration of military discipline and military justice, civilians and politicians had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The military disciplinary system was exclusively within the jurisdiction of the army. No political figure, or at least I do not know, had any authority or was responsible for military discipline, that is, pronounced punishment or something like that. Quite simply, they had no right, they had no powers to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just one final question, if I might introduce this as the last exhibit, Your Honours, just by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D212.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I'm sure there are many other examples of this, but we've just produced this as one example. You, as the brigade commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, actually had the authority, and you had the authority before the brigade was actually formed, to order arrests of soldiers on suspicion of having committed murder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. I see this order after many years. And even though it lacks the seal, but I can see my signature on it. I remember well those two soldiers. At that time, one must realize that there were quite a number of criminals around, and village thugs. And I believe this happened after a murder of which they were suspected of committing. Goran Medjugorac introduced himself as a member of HOS, Special Purpose Unit in Vitezovi, and Dragan Bilic, called Bambok [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you, that matter of detail is not important. I'm obliged to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I apologize to the Trial Chamber for tiptoeing over my time estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you what kind of murder were these two persons arrested for?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, from what I remember, I believe it was a murder which took place sometime around the 20th of October, murder of a TO soldier. I wouldn't know his last name. I think he was TO. After we talked to the commander of the TO headquarters in Zenica, I talked to them and I realised that they believed that it had been done by a group of soldiers who were trying to square some accounts I believe some debt was mentioned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, good afternoon. I'm Bozidar Kovacic, and with my colleague, lawyer Goran Mikulicic, I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. I shall ask you several questions. I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible, but I need to refer to some important things where I believe you can be of some help. Mr. Totic, you mentioned in your evidence -- and I should also like to tender a document to this effect -- you were the commander of a sector as of the 26th of November, 1992, at the front line between Turbe, that is, Gradina, to Strikanci, to hill feature 625, where Cerkez was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were designated to that sector on the orders from Blaskic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please help me distribute this document, and I should also like to ask for a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D68/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you look at that document, could you please confirm that this was the document designating you the commander of the mentioned sector?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this part of the front, which was under your responsibility, we also had some parts which were replenished from Vitez and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. About 200, 250 members of the Jure Francetic Brigade, the Vitez Brigade, which numbered some 60, 80, to 120, and the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, Novi Travnik, was some 150 to 200 men strong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Vitez Brigade", you are using this term conditionally, because at that time it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: The Vitez Brigade existed until the 4th of December. And after the reorganisation in the HVO, it was all one brigade, commanded by Borivoje Malbasic, and what came to be known as the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Earlier, and today also you mentioned that you met Mr. Cerkez. Could you tell us, please, when was that and what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Colonel Mario Cerkez I did meet sometime in August or maybe September 1992, after my assistants had informed me that Serb representatives of the village of Trnovlje, on the boundary between the municipalities of Vitez and Zenica, came to request HVO protection, and that in return they were ready to lay down their weapons. As the village was in the territory of the Vitez municipality, then I announced my visit to the command of the municipal headquarters there. And when I arrived there, I was met by the commander -- I believe it was Mr. Marijan Skopljak at the time -- and his deputy, Mr. Mario Cerkez, and that was the first time that I laid my eyes on Mr. Mario Cerkez. When I arrived, a representative of the local Serbs was already there. I believe his last name was Dzuric or Dzukic. And after that, in the war in 1993, 1994, I used to see him around Vitez. And I saw then that Mario Cerkez was talking about the protection of the local Serb population with that representative. And my information served only as an ancillary document. I saw that he was only taking care of that and that there was no need for me to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on. The problem of those Serbs with the HVO assistants in Vitez was resolved in a satisfactory manner, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I think it served -- that Vitez served as an example of the relations between local Serbs and local Croats. Throughout the war, local Serbs served in HVO units. I could ascertain it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you mentioned this village of Trnovlje specifically, which is on the boundary itself?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: But a little lower, Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Tolovici. And what you said also concerns Tolovici and other villages where there were Serbs in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August/September in 1992, in Vitez, at the time when you talked about it, the HVO was being organised by the municipal headquarters of the HVO Municipal Staff of the HVO in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but the HVO and the Municipal Staff existed then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time a brigade in Vitez did not exist yet, did it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those front lines were replenished with shifts of soldiers coming in from surrounding towns, depending on the sector for which people were responsible. Could we -- those shifts on the front, can we call them shift soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, not only were they shift soldiers; even brigades were only conditionally brigades. All those soldiers, after spending some eight to ten days on the front line, would go back home, would go back to their regular jobs, either in companies or in the field. We had no barracks, not a single one, in Central Bosnia, with the exception of Busovaca. But that was not the barracks; that was a depot. It could not accommodate people. So those soldiers from the front lines, with their rifles, went back home and then worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that status of troops, if one can call them troops, if one can call them soldiers, did it require a certain definition of the rules of conduct? The rules or regulations, when was somebody a soldier, when he was not a soldier? Let us take a soldier who served his shift above Turbe, at Kamenjas. He's in there for eight days, goes back to his village -- never mind whether it's Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, or what -- and at that day that he's back in the village, what is he then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: When he's come back to his village, he goes back to his regular activities, regular job. So at that moment, he ceases to be a soldier; he's a civilian. We did not have an army. It was an armed people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your experience and knowledge of this situation, would you know if that soldier that we just used as an example -- could he then also become part of village guards, which were also a frequent occurrence in villages?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Well, village guards existed in villages, but they were often not set up by any commanders, because they had their rifles with them and they themselves did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that moment, insofar as the HVO is concerned, the military wing of the HVO is concerned, they at that time were civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: At that period of time, they were civilians. That is, one becomes a soldier when he's with a military unit and is issued -- and is given a task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You mentioned a little while ago that on that occasion when you met Cerkez, you also met -- or rather you saw that he was talking to somebody called Djuric who was representing those villages. Let me ask you, in the course of that unfortunate war and after the Washington Accords, did you -- once again, did you ever have the opportunity, by a quirk of fate, to meet with Cerkez on a common task?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the Washington Accords were signed and after four or five months of preparation, the HVO and the army of BH invested joint efforts to undertake liberation operations in North-Western Bosnia. And as of that date, I believe that was as of the liberation of Kupres in November of '94, I began to meet Mr. Cerkez more often because we were involved in joint tasks in liberation operations. I was often in command of a battery of two shifts and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you remember if, in those operations or, rather, in the early days of those operations, the commander of engineers in Cerkez' unit was somebody, Gavro Mucibabic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Bosnian Serb from Vitez born in 1941. He was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean he was a Serb from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I think that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a high-ranking officer in Cerkez' unit?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more short question having to do with the area of responsibility that you had on a sector above Turbe. Will you agree with me that Cerkez organised the replenishment of shifts arriving from Vitez in a very -- very well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm that. Personally, while I was the commander and him my deputy, he performed his tasks very well indeed. After the incidents in Dusina, in Lasva, the HVO units in Zenica were not allowed to move towards Travnik, and as of that moment, Mr. Mario Cerkez took over the role of the commander, and I think he was that until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're referring to the sector?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Sector 2, defence from Turbe, Lasva, through Ostriglava [phoen], Rilja [phoen], Strikanci, Bacenja [phoen], including Kamenjas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against the army of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Against the army of Bosnian Serbs. In front of the front line, there were also two Muslim villages. The villages of Polac and Bijelo Bucje were in that area. During that period of time, I crossed the defence line. We daily removed clusters of mines on the road in order to let through parts of the BH army which were going over to take over shifts. And during all the time and later when Mario Cerkez commanded there, I do not know of any problems happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that even though there were tense relations and in Novi Travnik we had an open conflict, the HVO and ABiH still cooperate and still hold jointly the line against the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you notice that in these shifts which arrived from Vitez, there were a number of Serbs and Romanija in the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that in certain shifts, the number went to like 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Up to 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you mentioned today the 17th Krajina Brigade. You, of course, know that in the period during 1993, the commander of this powerful Muslim unit was Fikret Cuskic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I know when the 17th Krajina Brigade was first established, it's first commander was General Alagic, and Fikret Cuskic was its deputy. It was established in Borongaj in Croatian. It was armed by Croats, and it was sent to Bosnia to fight against the aggression of the Bosnian Serbs. Mr. Cuskic later became its commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so do I understand you correctly that it was established in Zagreb, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Borongaj barracks, and it was bussed to Travnik in some 20 buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time was it sent to Travnik from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what was the position or the rank or even status Mr. Cuskic had in Zagreb before coming to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: From what I heard, both Alagic and Fikret Cuskic had been members of the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean together?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, not only the two of them, but General Jasmin Jaganjac, Armin Pohara, and others. General Jaganjac was the military advisor to Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these men you have mentioned are Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were all in HV -- in the Croatian army before they joined the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct or should -- I should say do you know whether Fikret Cuskic was also a specialist for psychological warfare? This is what people --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: We in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone respected him as a very professional, very capable, and a very clever sort, and he was first in the 17th Krajina Brigade and then in the 7th Corps when it was eventually established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your general education and your military education, in particular, could you just confirm something for me. From some evidence which we have heard, the fall of Jajce on the 30th of October, 1992, caused both the Muslim and the Croat population, which means the soldiers coming from both of these ethnic groups, to flee to the south, and they arrived in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the assessment that the sudden influx of the defeated soldiers of both these sides, as well as the fleeing civilians, upset not only the statistical balance of the population at the time but also disrupted the supplies of livestock?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could anybody see this in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Anybody, not only a specialist, could see that throughout the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you mentioned that further to the HZ HB decision of 4 December, the HVO was reorganised. Do you recollect whether, in this reorganisation, the municipal HVO staffs were abolished and defence departments were established in municipalities as military agencies?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until the 4th of December, we had municipal staffs, and after 4th December, there were defence departments?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were territorially based?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being warned that I'm not waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In both cases, that is, the Municipal Staff and the Department of Defence were part of the civilian area, that is, political government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the defence department or our office is part of the municipal government, and the Department of Defence was regional and they were directly linked to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your evidence, you also mentioned an incident at the checkpoint near Cajdras where two HVO soldiers were killed and where the truck with Mujahedins was. Was this truck going to Vitez, carrying new equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was carrying military equipment to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the road where this incident took place, it passes through Poculica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Cajdras, Poculica, and at Vjetrenice it turns off towards two large villages, and later it turns out to strongholds of the ABiH, Lupac and Preocica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your conversations with Mr. Merdan during your trips and so on. Did he ever mention Cerkez as an enemy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: No. Dzemal Merdan never mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Totic, is it true that you and Cerkez went back to Jajce together in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the operations for liberation, I said that we were often involved in the same operations. And in '95, after the liberation of the town of Jajce, I turned over the control of the tactical group to Mario Cerkez, and I became commander of the town of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In closing, Mr. Totic, just one more thing. About 15 days ago, we saw on television that a memorial was erected to the fallen HVO soldiers, the soldiers who were killed on the 15th of April, and I think that I saw you there on television. You unveiled this monument; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, not only this, but I come from a country in which somebody is elected a president for the tearing down of a monument to the only noble laureate, and what am I to expect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was unveiled on the 15th of this last month?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then it was destroyed in six to seven hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that act also registered by television?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This will be a convenient moment to adjourn. Brigadier Totic, would you be back, please, on Monday morning at half past 9.00 to continue your evidence. Could you remember, during the adjournment, not to speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over, and that includes speaking to members of the Defence teams. Half past 9.00, then, on Monday, when I think we should be in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
